1.pericope_label: The four kings and the five; twelve years served, the thirteenth rebelled

schools.summary: Treat the chapter as an ancient document of foreign — probably Babylonian — origin, and use its antiquity to deny that the divine name proves late authorship; identify what can be identified from cylinders and comparative geography, and say plainly what cannot.

Canvass the identifications without settling them and doubt the classical framework outright; read the tribute as Noah’s prophecy taking effect, Canaan serving Shem; and set the whole war under the heads of Lot’s bad choice, God’s undeserved rescue, and the priesthood of Christ prefigured.
Note that the first war in scripture is recorded only because Abram and Lot were caught in it, and moralise the tribute — a rich country is a desirable prey, and its owners had small joy of it.
Follow the same reading of the invaders as colonial chiefs rather than great kings, fix the chronology of revolt and reprisal, and trace the servitude to Noah’s word about Canaan.

debates: Who Amraphel was: Nimrod (the Jewish writers, reported by Gill), Ninyas his grandson, a deputy governor of Shinar, or the bearer of an Accadian name meaning the circle of the year (Lenormant, in Ellicott).
Whether the four invaders were sovereign princes of Chaldea and Persia or merely heads of colonies settled near Sodom (Henry and Wesley take the second).
Whether the Babylonian and Assyrian kingdoms were yet of any consequence — Gill argues from scriptural silence that they were not.
Where Ellasar and Goyim were — Keil declines to settle either.
outliers: Ellicott alone turns the chapter’s antiquity into an argument against dating documents by the divine name they use.
Gill alone dismisses the classical accounts of Ninus and Semiramis as possibly mere fables.
Henry alone asks why the fifth king is left unnamed, and gives two opposite explanations.

5.pericope_label: Chedorlaomer’s campaign; the battle in the vale of Siddim

schools.summary: Identify the peoples and places from comparative geography and recent exploration; dispute whether the Rephaim were literally giants; explain the well’s name from a native custom of arbitration rather than from Israel’s later history; and read the topography for what it implies about the battle.
Gloss each name briefly from later scripture, flag the anachronistic tribal names, and derive the fountain of judgment from the rebellion of Moses and Aaron there.

Reject the derivation of the well’s name from a later event as a confusion of Moses’ time with Abram’s, read the march as a deliberate doubling back on the Amalekites, and explain the king of Sodom’s sortie by the possibility of retreat to the mountains.

debates: Whether the Rephaim were literally of gigantic stature (Keil: the one certain thing about them) or whether giants is a mistranslation in most places (Ellicott).

Why En-mishpat was called the fountain of judgment: from the judgment on Moses and Aaron (Clarke, and Jarchi and the Targum of Jonathan as reported by Gill), from its being the ancient native name of unknown origin (Gill’s own view), or from its use as a place of arbitration (Ellicott).
Whether the army returned by its own route or wheeled north-west (Ellicott) or doubled back deliberately on the Amalekites (Gill).
Whether the Zuzim can be identified with the Zamzummim — Clarke calls it conjecture, Ellicott treats it as established.
outliers: Ellicott alone identifies the goddess behind Ashteroth Karnaim and reports the excavation of the site.
Gill alone sets aside a rabbinic etymology on the ground that it reads Moses’ own later history back into Abram’s day.

10.pericope_label: The slimepits; the sack of Sodom; Lot carried away

schools.summary: Read the pits as natural bitumen springs and refuse the easy explanation that the kings blundered into them, arguing from the local knowledge they must have had and from the flight of the survivors that they threw themselves in out of terror; and take Lot’s capture as proof that nearness to the ungodly hastens the scourge.

Leave the manner of the fall open, note the Hebrew’s emphatic doubling of pits, classify the campaign as a predatory raid of a still-familiar kind, and press Lot’s fate as a warning by fable rather than by doctrine.
Take the pits for worked-out bitumen quarries rather than springs, and explain their military effect on a retreating army.

debates: Whether the slimepits were natural fountains of bitumen (Gill) or excavations from which bitumen had been dug (Ellicott).

How the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell there: by their own stratagem recoiling on them (Gill), by defeat and slaughter or by accident, left open (Clarke), by descending for safety (a view Calvin reports and rejects), or by deliberately choosing the pits over the sword (Calvin).
Whether Lot fought in the battle or was taken unarmed at home — Calvin argues the second from the order of Moses’ narrative.
outliers: Gill alone cites an eyewitness traveller for the present state of the pits.
Calvin alone reasons from the survivors’ flight to the mountains that those in the pits must have died.
Clarke alone illustrates the fate of the righteous among the wicked from Aesop rather than from scripture.

13.pericope_label: Abram the Hebrew arms three hundred and eighteen and rescues Lot

schools.summary: Derive Hebrew from crossing the river and refute the derivation from Eber outright; read the servants as both catechized and drilled; and dwell on the moral quality of the rescue — magnanimity toward an ungrateful kinsman, and tenderness toward the recovered women.
Take Hebrew as descent from Heber, in whose line true religion survived, and justify the expedition by its motive: charity, not gain, making it the most honourable war on record.

Ask whether a private man may lawfully war on kings and answer from Abram’s special calling and prior appointment as king of the land, or alternatively from the law of nations, Lot being a sojourner with no part in the quarrel; correct the verb armed, deny that trained means drilled, and settle the night attack as a division into several bands.

Hold both etymologies of Hebrew together and treat the title as preserved from the underlying document; affirm the military training from the standing danger to Abram’s herds; and read the geography of the pursuit to explain where it stopped.

debates: Whether the Hebrew means the man from beyond the river (Clarke, emphatically) or the descendant of Eber (Henry) — Ellicott takes both.
Whether trained servants means drilled soldiers (Ellicott), men formed from childhood by Abram’s discipline and faith (Calvin), or both together (Wesley).
What justified a private man in making war on kings: a special calling and heavenly command (Calvin) or the law of nations violated in seizing a sojourner (Gill).
What divided himself describes: Abram acting alone, a division of the allied bands, or a Hebraism for charging into the midst — Calvin lists all three and takes the second.
Who the escaped man was — Gill reports the rabbinic candidates only to reject them, Ellicott makes the word collective.
outliers: Clarke alone calls the absence of any earlier Hebrew among Eber’s descendants a demonstration against the patronymic.
Gill alone rests the justice of the war on Lot’s standing as a non-combatant sojourner.
Clarke alone notices the recovery of the women as an object of the narrator’s tenderness.

17.pericope_label: Melchizedek king of Salem; the blessing and the tithes

schools.summary: Rest the passage on the blessing: a priest of God sanctifying his inferior, which makes Melchizedek head of the whole Church and his priesthood the figure Christ fulfils; argue from the epistle that Abram paid rather than received the tithes, and take Melchizedek himself for a real Canaanite prince whose genealogy was concealed to make him a type.

Sweep away the conjectures and treat him as a historical king like the others named in the chapter; insist the bread and wine were refreshment and not sacrifice; and note that nearly all nations have devoted a tenth to religion.
Report both traditional identifications and press hard questions against the identification with Shem, while finding the description of him difficult to apply to any mere man.

Explain the Shem tradition as an attempt to reconcile Jewish readers to his superiority over Abraham; read the blessing as Hebrew poetry in parallel clauses; and prefer Onkelos on the origin of the king’s dale.

debates: Who Melchizedek was: Shem (the Targums, the rabbins, and many Christian writers), an appearance of the Son of God (many Christian writers, reported sympathetically by Henry), or a real Canaanite or Semitic king (Clarke, Gill, Ellicott). Wesley declines to decide.

Whether the bread and wine were refreshment or sacrifice — Clarke calls the sacrificial reading an idle conjecture; Wesley assigns the bread and wine to the kingly office and the blessing to the priestly.
Whether Abram paid the tithes or received them — Calvin has to refute the second reading before establishing the first.
Whether the tenth was of the spoils or of Abram’s own goods — Calvin leaves it open.
Whether the king of Sodom here is the Bera of verse 2 or a successor — Clarke and Keil agree he must be a successor, Bera having fallen in the battle.
outliers: Calvin alone draws from the blessing that Melchizedek was constituted head of the whole Church, and alone anticipates the objection that he blessed merely as a priest.
Gill alone lists the objection that Shem could not congratulate Abram on killing one of Shem’s own descendants.
Wesley alone suspends judgement on the identity, on the principle that what is not revealed cannot be determined.

21.pericope_label: The king of Sodom’s offer refused; from a thread to a shoelatchet

schools.summary: Take the king’s offer as sincere gratitude and treat the division of spoil as a prudent compounding of a genuinely disputed right.

Trace the gesture of the raised hand through the history of oath-taking, prefer a rabbinic reading of the proverb that takes in the rescued women, explain the refusal by the king’s scornful character, and preserve the allies’ right of conquest.

Suspect the king’s motive and read his humility as servile calculation; expound the oath’s form and direction while remaining uneasy that Abram swore at all; and defend Abram’s refusal as holy magnanimity rather than vanity, limited so as not to bind his allies.
Supply the customary rule of plunder that makes the offer unremarkable and Abram’s refusal exceptional, and read his detachment from the Amorites as the pattern of his descendants’ national policy.

debates: Whether the king of Sodom’s offer was gratitude (Henry, Wesley), the ordinary custom of dividing recovered plunder (Ellicott), or a calculating show of modesty by a man who had lost everything (Calvin).
What a thread denotes: a sewing thread or a hair lace (Gill) or a girl’s fillet, so that the proverb spans the rescued women and men (Clarke, from the rabbinical writers).
Whether Abram’s stated reason shows a mind too addicted to fame — Calvin raises the doubt and resolves it from the Spirit’s commendation.
Why the raised hand was used, and whether the practice was later displaced by another gesture (Clarke).
outliers: Ellicott alone makes the king’s offer conventional rather than generous, from Arab custom.
Calvin alone is uneasy that Abram took an oath at all.
Clarke alone wonders aloud whether Aner, Eshcol and Mamre proved as generous as Abram, and answers that we are not told.
Ellicott alone turns Abram’s refusal into a template for Israel’s foreign policy.
